questions.question: Should POST /orders be strictly limited and GET /orders get a separate, much higher budget, rather than leaving GET unlimited?

brief.where: PLAN.md calls GET cheap. src/orders.ts:16-18 selects every order row for the customer with no LIMIT and no pagination, so the tenant that created 40,000 orders now makes GET return 40,000 rows per call.
brief.what: Route scope decides whether the limit protects the read path. POST-only matches the plan and the incident, but the incident itself made GET expensive for exactly that customer, and a script hammering GET still saturates Postgres and the network.
brief.how: POST-only is the smallest change with one counter. Separate budgets means two counters and two numbers to defend. A shared budget lets enterprise polling eat the write allowance and break integrations.

evidence.note: listOrders has no limit or pagination
the plan's claim that GET is cheap

risks: If you add pagination to GET, POST-only becomes defensible again and this should be revisited.

options.label: POST strict, GET generous, separate budgets
options.description: Two counters, two sets of numbers.
options.tradeoff: Protects the read path your own incident made expensive; costs a second counter and a second number to justify to support.
options.cost: Two token buckets per customer; two limit values to define.

options.label: POST only
options.tradeoff: Smallest blast radius and matches the plan; leaves an unbounded per-customer full-table select unprotected.
options.cost: One counter; no change to the GET handler.

options.label: POST and GET share one budget
options.tradeoff: One number to explain; a customer's polling consumes their write allowance and will break integrations.
options.cost: One counter, but a semantics change callers did not expect.

questions.question: Should the limit be keyed on x-customer-id alone, accepting that the header is unauthenticated and spoofable?

brief.where: src/server.ts:7-8 requires x-customer-id and 401s without it, but nothing validates it. There is no X-Forwarded-For handling, and the LB is round-robin, so the peer address is likely the LB or an arbitrary instance.
brief.what: IP keying needs trusted-proxy configuration that does not exist, mis-keys customers behind shared egress, and lets a multi-IP customer escape. Customer-id keying matches the incident (a legitimate customer's script) but a rotating header creates a fresh bucket per request.
brief.how: Customer-id only needs no proxy work and no new identity source. IP-only survives header rotation but needs proxy trust and produces false positives. Both gives two counters per request and two different 429 reasons to explain.

evidence.note: identity comes from the header, unvalidated
customerId is passed straight through to the insert

risks: If nothing upstream authenticates the header, any limit keyed on it is advisory against a deliberate abuser.
Recording client IP behind the LB without trusted-proxy config records the LB's address.

options.label: x-customer-id alone
options.tradeoff: Matches the incident and needs no proxy work; costs nothing against a spoofing attacker, so it must be paired with the global backstop.
options.holds_when: The header is set by authenticated callers or by a trusted gateway.
options.cost: One key per customer.

options.label: Client IP alone
options.tradeoff: Survives header spoofing; costs false positives for shared egress and needs X-Forwarded-For trust config that does not exist.
options.holds_when: Every customer has dedicated egress IPs and the LB forwards the real address.
options.cost: Proxy config plus IP parsing.

options.label: Both: customer id and a per-IP cap
options.tradeoff: Catches both scripted bursts and header rotation; costs double Redis work and confusing double-429s for support.
options.cost: Two keys and two rejection paths.

questions.question: Should there also be a per-instance cap on concurrent POSTs, on top of the per-customer limit?

brief.where: The stated harm is that one customer slowed every other customer down. Per-customer limits bound one key, not aggregate write pressure, and a rotating or spoofed header multiplies keys. src/db.ts issues one insert per request with no visible pool bound.
brief.what: Rate limiting does not bound concurrency, which is what saturates Postgres connections and CPU. A per-instance in-flight cap is local, needs no Redis, and survives a Redis outage; a global Redis rate cap is one number but a hot key and another write-path dependency.
brief.how: Per-instance cap bounds each instance's pressure on Postgres and is trivial to implement. Global Redis cap bounds the total but shares the counter store's failure mode. No backstop leaves the original failure mode reachable.

evidence.note: every call goes straight to Postgres with no concurrency bound
the expensive path: JSON parse then insert

risks: Three instances mean aggregate concurrency is three times the per-instance cap.
A concurrency cap queues rather than rejects unless you also decide the timeout behaviour, which belongs to a later round.

options.label: Per-instance in-flight concurrency cap
options.description: A semaphore around the POST handler.
options.tradeoff: Bounds the resource that actually saturates, with no new dependency and no Redis on the backstop path; costs aggregate concurrency of 3x the cap and no bound on request rate.
options.cost: A counter in src/server.ts, roughly ten lines.

options.label: Global rate cap in Redis
options.description: One shared budget across all customers.
options.tradeoff: One total number that holds across instances; costs a hot key and another Redis dependency on the write path.
options.cost: A second Lua/atomic operation per POST.

options.label: No global backstop for v1
options.tradeoff: Least work and least new state; leaves many-customer or spoofed bursts unbounded.
options.cost: Nothing now, plus a follow-up incident risk.

questions.question: Should the limiter be a token bucket, so legitimate enterprise bursts up to a capacity are allowed and then refill at a sustained rate?

brief.where: 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst; the abusive script sustained about 66.7 orders per second for ten minutes. Any algorithm has to separate a short burst from a sustained flood.
brief.what: Fixed window is cheapest but admits up to twice the limit across a boundary and gives a poor Retry-After. A sliding-window log is exact but stores a timestamp per request per customer. Token bucket maps directly to burst capacity plus sustained refill and yields an exact time-to-next-token.
brief.how: Token bucket needs one atomic operation per request. Sliding log needs a sorted set per customer and trimming. Fixed window needs one counter and a key TTL. All three work in Redis; the choice changes the counter layout and the Retry-After answer.

evidence.note: bursty enterprise integrations and the expensive POST
40,000 orders in ten minutes, the sustained rate to stay under

risks: Capacity and refill numbers cannot be chosen until you have per-customer peak rates; that is a later round.

options.label: Token bucket
options.description: Capacity plus refill rate per key.
options.tradeoff: Expresses burst-then-sustained exactly and gives an exact Retry-After; costs an atomic script or a careful rollback on failure.
options.holds_when: Legitimate clients burst and you can define a burst size per customer.
options.cost: One Lua script and two numbers per limit tier.

options.label: Fixed window
options.description: Counter per minute with a TTL.
options.tradeoff: Simplest and cheapest to reason about; admits up to double the limit across a window boundary and makes Retry-After coarse.
options.cost: One INCR and one EXPIRE.

options.label: Sliding window log
options.description: Timestamp per request in a sorted set.
options.tradeoff: Exact smoothing with no boundary burst; memory grows with requests per window per customer.
options.cost: Sorted set per customer plus trimming on every call.

questions.question: Should the service team own default limits while support owns reviewed per-customer overrides in a table, rather than all numbers in code or self-serve editing?

brief.where: The plan leaves this open. There is no config file, admin surface, or limits table in the repo, and 20 enterprise customers will need higher limits.
brief.what: Ownership decides whether an enterprise exception costs a deploy, an ops ticket, or nothing, and whether an exception is auditable. Self-serve editing without review is how the 40,000-order incident gets recreated.
brief.how: Service defaults plus reviewed support overrides needs a small table and a cached read path. Code-only is auditable in git but serializes every exception through your release. Self-serve is fastest and least safe.

evidence.note: the open question as written
the only data access primitive available for a limits table

risks: Per-customer overrides read from Postgres on the hot path add a query per request unless cached.
Support cannot answer 'why am I getting 429' unless the response and logs name the limit; that is a later round.

options.label: Service team defaults, support owns reviewed overrides
options.description: Defaults in code, overrides in a table with an approver.
options.tradeoff: Enterprise exceptions ship without a deploy and every change is auditable; costs a table, a cache, and an approval step.
options.cost: One table, one cached read, one admin path.

options.label: Everything in code and config, changed by deploy
options.tradeoff: Auditable in git and no new state; every enterprise exception waits for a release, which may not fit this week.
options.cost: A deploy per exception.

options.label: Sales and support edit overrides directly
options.tradeoff: Fastest for customers; one mistyped zero recreates the incident.
options.cost: An admin surface with no gate.

brief.how: A 30-second cache means an override takes up to 30 seconds to apply on each instance and survives a Postgres blip with stale data. A per-request read is always fresh and slower. A Redis mirror is fastest and has the worst failure modes.

evidence.note: select is the only read primitive available
enterprise limits and rollout are unresolved

risks: Stale cache means support raises a limit and the customer still gets 429 for up to 30 seconds.
A table without an expires_at column makes temporary raises permanent.

options.label: Postgres table plus 30s in-memory cache with expires_at and audit columns
options.description: Row per customer, cached per instance.
options.tradeoff: No hot-path query and no new dependency, with time-bound and auditable exceptions; costs up to 30s staleness and a cache to invalidate.
options.cost: One table, one migration, a refresh timer in each instance.

options.label: Query the overrides table on every limited request
options.tradeoff: No staleness and simple reasoning; costs a Postgres round-trip before every POST, on the same database you are defending.
options.cost: One query per request, plus connection pressure.

options.label: Mirror overrides into Redis next to the counters
options.tradeoff: One round-trip and instant changes; costs a sync path and a second source of truth.
options.cost: An admin write path, a sync job, and drift monitoring.

questions.question: Should the limiter ship dark (count and log, no 429) for 24 to 48 hours, set enterprise overrides from that data, then enable enforcement behind a flag?

brief.where: Twenty enterprise integrations burst legitimately and there is no traffic record in the repo. Three instances behind a round-robin LB means a partial rollout covers an arbitrary third of traffic unless keyed by customer, not by instance.
brief.what: Dark mode produces the p99.9 data the numbers depend on and reveals which customers would have been 429ed. Enforcing immediately risks breaking an integration you did not know about, in the same week you are trying to stabilize the service.
brief.how: Dark then flip costs a day or two but preserves the ship date if the flag is in the first deploy. Immediate enforcement is fastest and least informed. Grandfathering the twenty enterprise customers removes their risk and leaves the largest bursters unmanaged.

evidence.note: the deadline and the incident that triggered this
three instances and twenty bursty enterprise customers

risks: A flag left off is a limiter that does nothing; the flag state needs an owner and an alert.
Per-instance rollout does not isolate customers under round-robin.

options.label: Ship dark 24-48h, set overrides from the data, then flip per instance
options.tradeoff: Safest and data-driven, and still inside the week; costs a flag, a review of the dark data, and a deliberate flip step.
options.holds_when: You can wait a day or two before enforcement starts.
options.cost: One config flag and a short review.

options.label: Enforce immediately with conservative defaults and contract-based overrides
options.tradeoff: The limit is active on day one; costs 429s on integrations whose real rates nobody measured.
options.cost: None extra, plus incident risk.

options.label: Enforce now for everyone except the twenty enterprise customers
options.tradeoff: Removes enterprise risk immediately; leaves the customers most likely to overwhelm Postgres unlimited.
options.cost: An allowlist and a later migration.

questions.question: Should the limiter emit structured JSON log lines per rejection and per fail-open plus a per-minute summary, with no new metrics infrastructure this week?

brief.where: There is no logging, metrics endpoint or telemetry dependency anywhere in src/. Support will be asked why a customer got 429, and the numbers decision depends on dark-mode data.
brief.what: Dark mode is worthless without a record of what would have been rejected per customer and per minute. Counters for allowed, rejected and fail-open, plus the observed rate, are the minimum to tune limits and to answer support.
brief.how: Structured logs need no dependency and work wherever stdout is collected. A metrics endpoint needs a dependency and a scrape config, and gives graphs but no per-customer detail unless labelled. No telemetry makes dark mode blind.

evidence.note: no logging or metrics anywhere in the server
the write path whose rate is being measured

risks: Per-request log lines at burst rates can themselves become load; log rejections and summaries, not every allowed request.
Customer ids in logs are a privacy question if the id maps to a person.

options.label: Structured JSON logs plus a per-minute summary
options.tradeoff: Ships this week and answers per-customer questions from logs; costs no dashboards and relies on whatever collects stdout.
options.cost: A logger call at rejection and a summary timer.

options.label: Add a /metrics endpoint with a client library
options.tradeoff: Graphable and alertable; costs a dependency, a scrape config, and label cardinality risk on customer ids.
options.cost: package.json, a metrics client, endpoint and scraping.

options.label: No telemetry
options.tradeoff: Least work; costs the ability to run dark mode or answer support, and makes tuning guesswork.
options.cost: Nothing now, unbounded later.

questions.question: Should the per-instance cap admit 32 concurrent POSTs, wait up to 250ms for a slot, then return 503 with Retry-After: 1?

brief.where: You chose a per-instance in-flight cap as the backstop. src/db.ts creates no pool, so every admitted request holds a Postgres connection for the duration of the insert.
brief.what: The cap value must fit inside Postgres max_connections divided by three instances, and that limit is not visible from the repo. Overflow behaviour decides whether clients see queueing latency or an immediate 503.
brief.how: A short wait smooths momentary spikes at the cost of tail latency. Immediate rejection is honest and cheap. Unbounded queueing turns overload into timeouts and connection pile-up.

evidence.note: one SQL client, no pool configuration visible
the handler that would hold a slot

risks: The number 32 is a placeholder until you read Postgres max_connections; three instances multiply it.
A 503 from the cap is a different client experience from a 429 from the bucket and needs documenting.

options.label: 32 in flight, 250ms wait, then 503 with Retry-After: 1
options.tradeoff: Absorbs brief spikes without pushing 503s; costs tail latency up to 250ms and a queue to implement.
options.holds_when: Postgres max_connections is comfortably above 96 plus other services.
options.cost: A semaphore with a timed wait.

options.label: Immediate 503 above the cap
options.tradeoff: Honest and trivial, with no latency added; costs 503s on momentary bursts that would have cleared.
options.cost: One counter and a branch.

options.label: Queue without a cap, rely on latency
options.tradeoff: No client-visible rejections; costs the original failure mode: unbounded connections and cross-customer slowdown.
options.cost: Nothing, and no protection.
